mathgap.title: Signed 'has more than' interpretation
mathgap.principle: Interpret any phrase of the form 'X has more than Y' as a signed difference X − Y = N, preserving the order given.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement says 'X has N more than Y', including when the phrase appears inside a larger clause.
mathgap.example: Reversing the sign and writing Ashlynn = Zelda + 58 for 'Zelda has 58 more broccolis than Ashlynn'.

mathgap.title: Model transfers as net changes
mathgap.principle: When a transfer 'X gives N to Y' occurs, subtract N from X and add N to Y, updating each person's count accordingly.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement explicitly says that one person gives a number of items to another.
mathgap.example: Subtracting 3 from Myles and adding 3 to Robert when the text says 'Robert gives 3 oranges to Myles'.

mathgap.title: Systematic equation solving
mathgap.principle: Introduce a distinct variable for each person and translate every relevant statement into a linear equation, then solve the resulting system.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After all statements have been parsed into equations, before extracting the answer.
mathgap.example: Leaving a relational statement untranslated and trying to guess the value directly.

mathgap.title: Signed difference phrasing
mathgap.principle: Interpret 'difference between X and Y' as the signed difference X − Y, preserving the order as presented.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement mentions the 'difference between' two persons.
mathgap.example: Treating 'difference between A and B' as |A − B| instead of A − B.

mathgap.title: Include transfers as constraints before solving relational equations
mathgap.principle: Apply all transfer statements first, updating each person's count, and then use those updated counts when translating relational equations.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Immediately after parsing direct counts, before handling any 'has more than' or 'difference' relations.
mathgap.example: Solving difference equations using the original counts and only later adjusting for transfers.

mathgap.title: Direct counts as initial constraints
mathgap.principle: Treat statements that give an explicit count (e.g., 'X has N items') as the initial amount before any transfers are applied.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement provides a concrete number for a person's items.
mathgap.example: Assuming a directly given count already includes the effect of later transfers.

mathgap.title: Answer formatting
mathgap.principle: Output the final answer using the exact required format: 'The final answer is $\boxed{<integer>}$'.
mathgap.example: Writing 'The answer is 23' instead of the required boxed format.

mathgap.title: Cluster independent sub-systems
mathgap.principle: Identify groups of variables that are only linked among themselves (no equations or transfers connecting them to other groups) and solve each cluster separately.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the system of equations is large and contains disconnected subsets.
mathgap.example: Attempting to solve the whole system at once without recognizing that some variables are unrelated to the target.

mathgap.title: Complex difference phrasing handling
mathgap.principle: For statements like 'the number of X that Y has more than Z is equal to the difference between the number of A and B', translate them as (Y − Z) = (A − B), preserving the order on both sides.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a relational statement combines 'has more than' with 'difference between' in a single sentence.
mathgap.example: Misreading 'the number of oranges that Adolfo has more than Taylor is equal to the difference between the number of oranges that James and Myles have' as Adolfo = Taylor + James + Myles.

mathgap.title: Transfer with unknown counts handling
mathgap.principle: When a transfer involves a person whose count is not directly given, introduce a separate variable for their pre‑transfer amount, apply the transfer to define a post‑transfer variable, and use the post‑transfer variable in all subsequent relational equations.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a transfer statement mentions a giver or receiver without an explicit count.
mathgap.example: Treating Henry's final count as an unknown and directly using it in equations without accounting for the 52‑item transfer he gave away.

mathgap.description: Treating direct count statements as final counts after transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes that a given count already reflects any later transfers, ignoring that transfers modify the amounts.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Record direct counts as initial values, then apply all transfer adjustments before using those numbers in relational equations.

mathgap.description: Applying transfers in the wrong direction
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model confuses the giver and receiver, subtracting from the receiver or adding to the giver.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: When a statement says 'X gives N to Y', subtract N from X's count and add N to Y's count.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model treats conditional phrasing as unconditional, or fails to enforce the condition.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Identify the condition explicitly; only apply the transfer if the condition holds, otherwise leave counts unchanged.

mathgap.description: Misinterpreting signed difference statements as absolute differences
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model drops the sign and treats 'difference between X and Y' as |X − Y|, losing the order information.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Preserve the order given: translate 'difference between X and Y' to X − Y, not the absolute value.

mathgap.description: Failing to introduce pre‑ and post‑transfer variables for persons with unknown counts in transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: When a giver or receiver lacks a direct count, the model tries to use a single variable for both pre‑ and post‑transfer amounts, mixing the two stages.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Create two variables (pre‑transfer and post‑transfer) for such persons; link them with the transfer amount, and use the post‑transfer variable in all later equations.
